summary.title: Evidence Based Scheduling
summary.one_liner: Learn how Evidence-Based Scheduling (EBS) turns historical timesheet velocities into a Monte Carlo confidence curve of ship dates, rather than a single optimistic date.
keywords: how to predict software ship date
takeaways: Break work into tasks no longer than 16 hours so estimates are concrete.
Track estimate versus actual time per task to compute a velocity history per developer, discarding data older than about six months.
Run a Monte Carlo simulation that divides each estimate by randomly sampled historical velocities to get a probability distribution of ship dates.
Leave interruptions on the active task's clock instead of estimating them separately; EBS absorbs them into velocity.
Use nightly snapshots of the 5%, 50% and 95% ship-date curves to see whether the schedule is converging or slipping, and cut features when the box of work does not fit.
summary.summary: Joel Spolsky describes Evidence-Based Scheduling, a method developed at Fog Creek, that uses historical timesheet data to forecast software ship dates. Developers break work into tasks under 16 hours, record actual times, and compute velocities (estimate divided by actual). The article then runs through a Monte Carlo simulation over these velocities to produce a confidence curve of possible ship dates, with worked examples for perfect, bad, and typical estimators. It closes with advice on managing scope, buffers, and cutting features, and notes that EBS is built into FogBugz 6.0.
